content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Technical deep dive - tail latency + KV cache behavior (Dedicated eval)
Date: 2025-02-14
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Omar El-Sayed, Hiro Tanaka, Sean Gallagher
HelioFin: Priya Desai, Max Chen, Elena Novak, Jordan Wells

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioFin shared concerns about bursty p99 latency spikes observed in their current setup and asked how Redwood Dedicated handles tail latency under mixed context lengths.
- Redwood explained root causes seen in production: KV cache fragmentation under mixed prefill/decode and burst routing, plus allocator churn and occasional allocation failures.
- Redwood previewed upcoming KV cache compaction strategy: block-based allocator with movable segments, scheduler-aware eviction, and budgeted compaction triggers behind a runtime flag.
- Discussed observability signals, canary/rollback plan, and how Dedicated pools isolate noisy neighbors.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Tail latency SLOs (p95/p99) and burst handling
- KV cache fragmentation mechanics
- Eviction policy + scheduler contract
- Compaction triggers and budgeting
- Dedicated pool sizing, admission control, and OOM risk
- Metrics/dashboards and incident response

Action items (auto-generated)
- Lauren to send Dedicated architecture + sizing note for HelioFin workloads
- Omar to share fragmentation/compaction metrics spec and how to interpret it
- Max to provide prompt/decode distribution and burst arrival assumptions
- Sean to share suggested alert thresholds + rollback checklist used for canaries

---
Transcript

[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Cool, yeah, thanks everyone for making the time. This is the technical deep dive Max and Priya asked for—tail latency, KV cache, the stuff that usually doesn’t make it into the normal sales deck.

[00:12] Priya Desai: Great. Yeah, we’re… we’re basically trying to de-risk p99. Like our average is fine. It’s the spikes that take out our downstream SLAs.

[00:22] Lauren Bishop: Understood. Quick intros? Lauren, I run product for Dedicated.

[00:26] Omar El-Sayed: I’m Omar, I lead KV cache and memory management in the serving runtime.

[00:31] Hiro Tanaka: Hiro, kernel performance, attention, all that.

[00:34] Sean Gallagher: Sean, SRE for runtime rollouts and incident response.

[00:38] Max Chen: Max, ML infra. I’m the one who gets paged when GPUs go sideways.

[00:43] Elena Novak: Elena, SRE on our side.

[00:45] Jordan Wells: Jordan, security.

[00:48] Lauren Bishop: Perfect. So, Priya, can you give the 30-second version of what you’re seeing today?

[00:55] Priya Desai: Sure. We do LLM-based support summarization and some agent-y workflows. Traffic is spiky. Like 10x bursts around top of hour and also when a batch job completes. We’re on… currently we’ve tried Azure OpenAI and a self-hosted thing with vLLM. Average latency is okay. But p99 sometimes jumps from like 800ms to 6, 7 seconds. That kills us.

[01:19] Max Chen: And we suspect it’s memory thrash. Like, GPU memory looks fine until it doesn’t. Then you see allocation retries, sometimes OOM, then it recovers.

[01:29] Lauren Bishop: Got it. That’s basically the exact bucket this call is about.

[01:34] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. So I’ll start with a simplified mental model and then we can go deep. In decode, your speed mostly depends on KV cache behavior. Each active sequence consumes KV cache pages/blocks for each layer. Under bursty load, you have lots of sequences entering and exiting; some finish quickly, some are long contexts. If allocation is not compact, you get holes.

[01:58] Priya Desai: Holes like fragmentation.

[02:00] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. Fragmentation increases the overhead of “finding” contiguous free space or enough blocks. And more importantly, it increases the probability you hit the “I technically have free memory but not in the right shape” problem.

[02:14] Elena Novak: Is that a driver-level fragmentation or your allocator?

[02:18] Omar El-Sayed: In our case it’s mostly at the KV cache allocator layer. We use a block map on top of GPU allocations. The raw GPU allocation is large, but within it, blocks can get unevenly utilized.

[02:31] Hiro Tanaka: And to connect it to latency: when we can’t place a new sequence quickly, we either do an eviction, or we stall scheduling. That pushes p95/p99.

[02:42] Max Chen: So you’re saying the tail is allocator overhead, not compute.

[02:46] Hiro Tanaka: Often it’s both. The compute path is stable. The unstable part is admission, paging, eviction, synchronization points—anything that forces you to wait.

[02:58] Lauren Bishop: And just to anchor: in Dedicated, you’re not sharing that pool with other tenants. But you can still have internal fragmentation based on your own traffic mix.

[03:10] Priya Desai: That’s helpful, because we were worried about noisy neighbors.

[03:14] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated solves noisy neighbors. It doesn’t solve physics.

[03:18] (crosstalk)

[03:19] Priya Desai: Yeah fair.

[03:21] Max Chen: Ok, so what does Redwood do today, like right now, before the “upcoming compaction” thing?

[03:29] Omar El-Sayed: Today we have: (1) allocator with free lists, (2) eviction when we hit pressure, (3) some admission control. And we’ve got prefix caching in some paths which changes reuse, but not always.

[03:43] Max Chen: And eviction means you drop sequences?

[03:46] Omar El-Sayed: Not drop customer requests, but we may evict cached KV for sequences we predict won’t be reused, or in worst case we reduce concurrency by backpressuring new requests. In a strict sense: we avoid corruption; correctness is maintained, but latency goes up.

[04:03] Elena Novak: When you say “predict won’t be reused,” is that like prompt prefix reuse?

[04:08] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, prefix KV reuse. If you have a shared system prompt or similar. But in many agent workflows the reuse is less straightforward.

[04:17] Priya Desai: So where are your p99 spikes coming from in your environment?

[04:22] Sean Gallagher: We’ve had a couple incidents where a region had bursty arrivals plus mixed sequence lengths, and we saw increased allocator failures—like, allocation succeeded but after multiple scans, and eviction churn. That correlated directly with p99.

[04:38] Lauren Bishop: We did a postmortem on one in February—can share sanitized learnings.

[04:45] Jordan Wells: Sanitized is good.

[04:47] Lauren Bishop: Yep.

[04:49] Max Chen: Okay. So compaction. What’s the strategy—are you doing like defrag, moving blocks around on GPU memory? Sounds scary.

[04:59] Omar El-Sayed: It is scary. That’s why it’s behind a feature flag and has budgets. But yes, the plan is to make blocks movable at the allocator level.

[05:09] Max Chen: Movable meaning you copy KV pages?

[05:12] Omar El-Sayed: Correct. Conceptually: take a partially-filled region and pack it so you have larger contiguous free ranges (or fewer partially used segments). There are a few approaches—slab allocators, two-tier hot/cold, paging—our current direction is a page/block allocator with move semantics.

[05:32] Hiro Tanaka: The kernel side cares because addresses/pointers to KV cache must remain consistent during a decode step. So you need synchronization so you don’t move memory while a kernel is reading it.

[05:45] Priya Desai: Right, that’s what I was going to ask. If you move it, how do you not break in-flight decode?

[05:51] Hiro Tanaka: You can’t move it in-flight. We do moves at safe points—between steps, with stream sync boundaries. There’s a lot of detail there.

[06:00] Omar El-Sayed: Another way to say it: compaction happens in small increments, scheduled, not “stop the world and defrag for 200ms.”

[06:10] Max Chen: But even small increments—copying on GPU—still costs.

[06:14] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. That’s why the compaction trigger is budgeted. For example: “at most X microseconds per second” or “at most Y bytes moved per N tokens” type budget. We’re still finalizing the best formulation.

[06:31] Elena Novak: Do you have a metric you’ll expose for that? Like compaction time spent.

[06:36] Sean Gallagher: Yes. We’re adding fragmentation ratio, eviction rate, allocation failures, and compaction cost counters. We can break them down by pool and model family.

[06:48] Priya Desai: Fragmentation ratio—what’s the definition? We’ve seen like five different ones.

[06:53] Omar El-Sayed: Totally fair. Ours is basically “free blocks that are unusable for typical allocation sizes” divided by total free blocks. We’ll publish the exact formula in the metrics doc. It’s designed to correlate with allocation churn more than with theoretical free memory.

[07:11] Max Chen: So you’re measuring unusable free space, not just total free.

[07:14] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly.

[07:17] Lauren Bishop: Maybe it’s helpful to connect this to your Dedicated decision. Today, without compaction, we can still size a pool so you’re far from pressure most of the time, which reduces tails. With compaction, you can get better utilization and reduce tails under burst.

[07:35] Priya Desai: Our fear is we pay for dedicated and still get spikes.

[07:40] Lauren Bishop: The honest answer is: you will always have some tails under extreme burst. The question is whether tails are within your error budget, and whether they’re predictable and observable.

[07:52] Elena Novak: Observable is huge for us. Like, we need to know “it’s cache pressure” not “the GPU is haunted.”

[08:00] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Part of the work is surfacing the signals so oncall can say: fragmentation is rising, compaction is hitting budget, eviction is spiking. Then you take mitigations: temporarily lower max concurrency, adjust admission, or in Dedicated you can increase reserved capacity.

[08:18] Max Chen: Is there an automatic fallback? Like routing to a smaller model if you’re under pressure.

[08:23] Lauren Bishop: On Hosted we do more policy routing. On Dedicated we typically keep you pinned, but we can discuss “graceful degradation” options if you want. Usually customers prefer consistency.

[08:35] Priya Desai: Yeah, we prefer consistency.

[08:37] Omar El-Sayed: There’s also an eviction policy piece. Compaction reduces holes, but eviction policy determines which sequences lose cache when under pressure. We’re making that scheduler-aware.

[08:51] Priya Desai: Scheduler-aware how?

[08:54] Omar El-Sayed: The scheduler knows tenant tier, request priority, age, maybe SLA class. Under pressure, eviction shouldn’t starve low-priority forever, but it also shouldn’t evict your most expensive-to-recompute state.

[09:12] Max Chen: That sounds complicated.

[09:14] Omar El-Sayed: It is. That’s why we’re explicitly defining a contract between scheduler and cache. Like: scheduler provides a priority class, cache reports pressure, scheduler decides whether to admit new work or slow down.

[09:28] Hiro Tanaka: Also it’s important that eviction/compaction doesn’t regress median latency. You can “fix p99” by making everything slower; that’s not acceptable.

[09:39] Priya Desai: Right.

[09:41] Lauren Bishop: If it’s okay, can we ask about your workload shape? Specifically context lengths and output tokens.

[09:48] Max Chen: Yeah. Typical prompt is 2k to 6k tokens, but we have some 20k-ish. Output is like 200 to 800 tokens. Bursts are mostly many small-ish jobs but mixed. The long ones make it weird.

[10:05] Omar El-Sayed: That mix is exactly the fragmentation trigger. Long contexts hold blocks longer, short ones free quickly, so you get holes of different sizes.

[10:15] Elena Novak: In your incident you mentioned “mixed prefill/decode.” Is that when you’re doing continuous batching?

[10:21] Hiro Tanaka: Yes. Continuous batching interleaves prefill and decode. Prefill allocates a bunch of KV upfront; decode adds incrementally. The allocator sees different patterns and can end up with scattered free blocks.

[10:36] Max Chen: Does the model architecture matter? Like, llama vs mistral etc.

[10:40] Hiro Tanaka: It matters in KV size per token per layer, so yes. Also kernel selection and page size alignment can matter.

[10:49] Priya Desai: You mentioned page size earlier. What is it today?

[10:53] Omar El-Sayed: Today we use a block size tuned for throughput and metadata overhead, but we’re revisiting it for compaction. Bigger blocks reduce metadata but increase internal waste; smaller blocks reduce waste but increase pointer chasing and management overhead.

[11:11] Max Chen: So you’re doing that tradeoff analysis now.

[11:14] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly.

[11:17] Jordan Wells: Quick security question: in Dedicated, do you ever move our KV into a shared memory region or across tenants during compaction.

[11:26] Lauren Bishop: No. Dedicated is single-tenant at the pool level. Compaction is within your pool’s device memory. There is no cross-tenant memory sharing.

[11:36] Jordan Wells: Okay.

[11:38] Sean Gallagher: And from an ops perspective, telemetry about fragmentation is aggregate counters; we’re not logging prompts.

[11:47] Jordan Wells: We’ll still want to see the logging retention policy, but fine.

[11:52] Lauren Bishop: Yep, we can send the standard.

[11:55] Priya Desai: Can we get more concrete on “tail latency improvement”? Like do you have a number.

[12:02] Omar El-Sayed: I’m going to be careful because it depends on workload. But for the workloads where fragmentation is the dominant tail driver, we’ve seen p99 spikes reduce materially in internal tests. Think “spikes flatten,” not “every request gets 2x faster.”

[12:20] Max Chen: But you have some baseline.

[12:22] Omar El-Sayed: We’re building a benchmark suite that has bursty arrival and mixed lengths. In that suite we’re targeting measurable p95/p99 improvements and lower allocator failure rate. I can share the methodology, not the exact numbers until we run your shape.

[12:40] Priya Desai: That’s fair. We just need enough to make a decision.

[12:44] Lauren Bishop: The way we typically do it is: we set up a Dedicated PoC pool, run your traffic replay or synthetic approximation, and look at p95/p99 and error rates. Then you can decide.

[12:58] Elena Novak: Do you have a way to simulate the burst? Like ramp quickly.

[13:02] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, we can do that in the perf harness. We can also do a replay that has “top of hour” burst patterns.

[13:12] Max Chen: How does admission control behave during burst? Does it queue or reject?

[13:17] Lauren Bishop: Typically queue with backpressure; you can configure timeouts. On Hosted, sometimes we shed load based on tenant tier. On Dedicated, it’s your choice—queue depth, max in-flight.

[13:31] Priya Desai: We’d prefer queue over reject, but our upstream has a hard timeout.

[13:36] Sean Gallagher: Then we tune max queue time and we keep an eye on tail.

[13:41] Hiro Tanaka: Also worth noting: if you queue too much, you turn burst into sustained load, which can make cache pressure persist.

[13:50] Max Chen: Yep, seen that.

[13:53] Priya Desai: Let’s go back to compaction safety. What’s the worst case? Like, could it crash the runtime.

[14:00] Omar El-Sayed: Worst case we’re designing against is corruption, which is unacceptable. So we have a bunch of safety invariants: don’t move blocks referenced by in-flight kernels; move only at safe points; maintain a versioned mapping; and a kill-switch flag.

[14:18] Elena Novak: Kill-switch as in you can turn it off without redeploy.

[14:21] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Feature flag per pool/region. If we see regressions, we disable it.

[14:28] Max Chen: How quickly does it take effect.

[14:30] Sean Gallagher: Minutes. Depending on config propagation. Not like hours.

[14:36] Priya Desai: And you said budgeted. So if compaction is too expensive it just stops.

[14:42] Omar El-Sayed: Right. It should never “run away.” If it hits budget, it defers.

[14:49] Hiro Tanaka: And compaction triggers can be threshold-based: if fragmentation exceeds some ratio, or on allocation failure fallback.

[14:58] Max Chen: Allocation failure fallback is basically “oh crap, compact now.”

[15:02] Omar El-Sayed: Within a tight bound, yes.

[15:05] Priya Desai: That sounds like it could still create a latency spike.

[15:09] Omar El-Sayed: Which is why we do it before you’re in crisis—threshold triggers.

[15:14] Sean Gallagher: And we alarm on rising fragmentation early.

[15:18] Elena Novak: What are the alarms.

[15:20] Sean Gallagher: Tentatively: fragmentation ratio crossing X for Y minutes, allocation failure > 0.1% requests, compaction time hitting budget consistently, and of course p99 regressions.

[15:36] Lauren Bishop: We’ll share the exact thresholds we use in canaries.

[15:40] Priya Desai: Okay.

[15:42] Max Chen: You mentioned eviction policy fairness. Can you explain that quickly.

[15:48] Omar El-Sayed: Sure. Imagine you have priority classes: interactive user traffic vs batch. Under pressure, you want batch to be slowed first, but not starved forever. Also, you don’t want one long sequence to cause repeated eviction of many short sequences—thrash. So we track per-tenant or per-class consumption and apply constraints.

[16:10] Priya Desai: In Dedicated, do you mean “tenant” as in our internal apps.

[16:13] Omar El-Sayed: Could be. You can tag traffic by route/key, depending on integration.

[16:20] Max Chen: Got it.

[16:22] Lauren Bishop: We’re at ~16 minutes. We can spend the rest either on (A) deeper technical specifics, or (B) practical PoC plan and success criteria.

[16:31] Priya Desai: I want both, but maybe PoC success criteria first.

[16:35] Lauren Bishop: Great. For Dedicated evals, we usually define: p95, p99 under normal and burst; error rate/timeouts; and cost/throughput. Also operational: do the metrics tell a coherent story.

[16:52] Elena Novak: Add “no pager storms.”

[16:54] Lauren Bishop: Yes.

[16:56] Max Chen: For us, we need p99 under 2 seconds at burst, and under 1 second steady. That’s rough.

[17:05] Hiro Tanaka: Which model size are you targeting.

[17:08] Max Chen: Likely a 70B class for some tasks, but we might do 8B for others.

[17:14] Hiro Tanaka: Mixed model sizes complicate pooling. You might want separate pools.

[17:20] Lauren Bishop: In Dedicated we can do that. Two pools or multi-queue.

[17:24] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:26] Max Chen: Now the technical: what’s your current view on block size and pointer stability.

[17:33] Omar El-Sayed: Pointer stability: we maintain an indirection. Kernels don’t keep raw addresses long-term. There’s a mapping table that can be updated at safe points.

[17:44] Max Chen: So there’s a level of indirection always.

[17:47] Hiro Tanaka: In practice yes, though we keep it optimized. There’s a performance tradeoff.

[17:53] Omar El-Sayed: Block size is under discussion. Larger blocks: fewer map entries, faster lookups, but more internal fragmentation. Smaller blocks: better packing, more metadata overhead.

[18:07] Priya Desai: And compaction moves blocks—so moving smaller blocks is more operations.

[18:11] Omar El-Sayed: Right. But each move is smaller.

[18:14] Max Chen: What about the GPU copy itself. Is it device-to-device memcpy.

[18:19] Hiro Tanaka: It’s GPU memcopy, but you need to synchronize with compute streams. So the copy can contend if not planned.

[18:28] Max Chen: That’s where budget comes in.

[18:30] Hiro Tanaka: Exactly.

[18:33] Elena Novak: I’m thinking about worst-case tail. If a request arrives exactly when you hit a compaction safe point, it might wait.

[18:41] Sean Gallagher: That can happen. The goal is to minimize it and keep it bounded. Also, we’d prefer to do compaction work when the scheduler is already backpressuring, so you don’t add delay on top of a fast path.

[18:57] Priya Desai: That’s scheduler-aware too.

[19:00] Omar El-Sayed: Yes.

[19:02] Lauren Bishop: There’s also “compaction vs eviction” choice. Sometimes it’s cheaper to evict cold blocks than to compact.

[19:12] Max Chen: How do you decide cold.

[19:14] Omar El-Sayed: Request age, likelihood of reuse, class. We’re not doing fancy ML prediction; it’s heuristics.

[19:24] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:26] Jordan Wells: Just confirming: no customer data is stored outside the pool. And in Dedicated, you support customer-managed keys.

[19:35] Lauren Bishop: Yes. KMS integration available for Dedicated and Private; audit logs as well. We can do a separate security review call.

[19:44] Jordan Wells: Cool.

[19:46] Max Chen: Back to latency. Do you have a graph of fragmentation vs p99.

[19:52] Sean Gallagher: We do internally. We can share a sanitized screenshot or description. The dashboard panel basically overlays p99 with fragmentation ratio and allocation failures.

[20:04] Elena Novak: That’s what we want.

[20:06] Priya Desai: When is compaction shipping.

[20:09] Omar El-Sayed: We’re implementing now. Earliest canary is a couple weeks. General rollout after that if stable.

[20:18] Max Chen: So not GA today.

[20:20] Lauren Bishop: Correct. For your PoC, we can run without it first, then if timing lines up, we can test with it enabled behind the flag in your pool.

[20:31] Priya Desai: That’s acceptable.

[20:33] Max Chen: But we need to decide soon.

[20:35] Lauren Bishop: Understood. We can still mitigate tails via sizing and policy even before compaction.

[20:43] Hiro Tanaka: For example, keep a higher headroom in KV cache, reduce maximum batch size under burst, things like that.

[20:51] Max Chen: That’s basically paying for headroom.

[20:54] Lauren Bishop: Yes. Compaction is about reducing how much headroom you need.

[21:00] Priya Desai: That’s a good framing.

[21:02] Elena Novak: Can we talk about rollback. If compaction causes issues, what happens.

[21:08] Sean Gallagher: Rollback is disable flag, and optionally restart workers if needed. But we’re designing it so disable flag is enough. We also have an escalation path: page runtime oncall.

[21:22] Priya Desai: Do you have an oncall for Dedicated pools.

[21:26] Sean Gallagher: Yes, Dedicated has an oncall rotation and SLO monitoring. We can define SLA targets in contract.

[21:35] Priya Desai: Okay.

[21:37] Max Chen: How do you isolate model versions. We don’t want change mid-quarter.

[21:42] Lauren Bishop: You can pin runtime + model versions in Dedicated. We do controlled upgrades.

[21:48] Max Chen: Good.

[21:50] Hiro Tanaka: And the compaction flag is opt-in initially.

[21:54] Priya Desai: That’s important.

[21:56] Lauren Bishop: Can I ask: what are you using as a competitor baseline. You mentioned Azure OpenAI and self-hosted.

[22:03] Priya Desai: We tried Bedrock too. Together AI is in the mix. Anyscale pitched us on a managed thing.

[22:10] Lauren Bishop: Okay.

[22:12] Max Chen: The issue with the managed ones is we can’t see anything when it goes wrong. Like no cache metrics.

[22:18] Sean Gallagher: That’s a common pain. We’ll give you per-pool metrics including cache health.

[22:26] Elena Novak: And logs.

[22:27] Sean Gallagher: Structured logs for cache events, not content.

[22:31] Priya Desai: Great.

[22:33] Omar El-Sayed: Maybe I’ll do a short “what fragmentation looks like” narrative. Say you have block size of B tokens. A long sequence uses many blocks and holds them. Short sequences finish and free blocks scattered across the address space. Now when a new long sequence arrives, it needs N blocks. You have N blocks free, but they’re fragmented. Allocator scans, tries to assemble a run; if it’s expensive, you stall. If you fail, you evict and retry. That’s the churn.

[23:02] Max Chen: That matches what we see in vLLM sometimes.

[23:05] Omar El-Sayed: Yep. Then compaction says: take those scattered free blocks and pack active blocks to make the free space contiguous. Now the next long sequence can allocate quickly.

[23:18] Priya Desai: Does compaction ever move active sequences that are decoding.

[23:22] Omar El-Sayed: Not mid-step. Only at boundaries.

[23:27] Hiro Tanaka: There’s nuance: prefill can be long, too. But there are defined safe points.

[23:34] Max Chen: Okay.

[23:36] Elena Novak: What’s the cost of compaction relative to decode.

[23:41] Hiro Tanaka: It’s workload dependent. Copying KV is bandwidth-bound. If you move too much you’ll steal bandwidth from compute. So we cap it.

[23:54] Priya Desai: So again budget.

[23:56] Hiro Tanaka: Yes.

[23:58] Lauren Bishop: I’m watching time. We should also cover what you need from us to run a PoC.

[24:04] Max Chen: We can give you distributions. We can’t share raw prompts.

[24:08] Lauren Bishop: That’s fine. Token histograms and arrival patterns are enough to start.

[24:14] Priya Desai: We can also run a synthetic generator on our side.

[24:17] Lauren Bishop: Great.

[24:19] Sean Gallagher: One thing to add: if you want to compare apples to apples, we should also capture “timeouts due to queueing” vs “timeouts due to compute.” Our metrics break that down.

[24:31] Elena Novak: Nice.

[24:33] Max Chen: I’d like to know if the spikes are allocator vs scheduler.

[24:37] Omar El-Sayed: We’re adding per-request attribution where possible. Like, was the request delayed due to allocation retry, eviction, compaction, or just queue.

[24:49] Max Chen: That’s great, but is it available now.

[24:52] Omar El-Sayed: Some of it is. The more detailed attribution is part of the work in progress.

[24:58] Priya Desai: Okay.

[25:00] Jordan Wells: Not to derail, but does any of that per-request logging contain identifiers.

[25:06] Sean Gallagher: It can include request IDs and timing, but not prompt content. In Dedicated we can configure retention.

[25:13] Jordan Wells: Okay.

[25:15] Priya Desai: Another question: if we have two traffic classes—interactive and batch—can we guarantee interactive doesn’t get blown up by batch.

[25:25] Lauren Bishop: Yes, via separate pools or scheduler priorities within a pool.

[25:30] Omar El-Sayed: Scheduler priorities is part of the eviction contract I mentioned. It’s not just CPU queue priority; it influences cache pressure decisions.

[25:41] Max Chen: Would you recommend separate pools.

[25:43] Lauren Bishop: Often yes, for isolation.

[25:46] Elena Novak: Separate pools means more cost.

[25:49] Lauren Bishop: True. We can model it.

[25:52] Max Chen: Okay.

[25:54] (brief silence)

[25:56] Priya Desai: Can you speak to OOM risk. Like our long-context jobs sometimes cause OOM when we increase concurrency.

[26:04] Omar El-Sayed: OOM risk increases when you run near the edge and fragmentation reduces effective free space. Compaction reduces that risk by making memory usable. Also we can enforce per-request limits or admission that accounts for worst-case token growth.

[26:23] Hiro Tanaka: And you can also cap max context or route long-context to a separate pool.

[26:29] Max Chen: We can do that.

[26:31] Sean Gallagher: From SRE: we’d rather you have deterministic backpressure than nondeterministic OOM. OOM creates long recovery and unpredictable tails.

[26:41] Priya Desai: Agree.

[26:43] Lauren Bishop: Okay, I want to make sure we answer the “when will this be stable” question. Omar, what’s your confidence.

[26:50] Omar El-Sayed: Confidence is high on correctness with the safety constraints, but we’re still tuning budgets to avoid median regression. That’s why we do canaries.

[27:03] Priya Desai: That’s honest.

[27:05] Max Chen: And you’ll run canary in one region first.

[27:09] Sean Gallagher: Yes, and also one Dedicated pool internally. We gate on p99 and allocator failure rate.

[27:18] Elena Novak: Good.

[27:20] Lauren Bishop: For your timeline, if we start PoC next week, we can get baseline results quickly. Then we can decide whether to wait for compaction or size with headroom.

[27:33] Priya Desai: Okay.

[27:35] Max Chen: One more technical: do you do anything like memory pooling across GPUs or is it per GPU.

[27:42] Omar El-Sayed: KV cache is per GPU. For tensor parallel you’ll have shards.

[27:48] Max Chen: Okay.
